§11.2.3 Gantt and Sankey Charts

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

charts-gantt-and-sankey-charts · charts types

✅ Normative

A gantt chart MUST be rendered with one row per mark, giving the mark's label, its start and its end on the time axis — for a milestone, start and end are the same period. A sankey diagram MUST be rendered with one row per flow, giving its source node, its target node and the value it carries. Each family uses its one shape throughout, whatever the chart prints.

Gantt

The time axis is the value axis. Each bar's two edges are read against the printed ticks and written as the periods the axis prints: months as month tokens (Jan), quarters under year headers as quarter tokens with their year (Q1 2025). When the page prints exact dates for each task, those printed dates are the start and end; when it prints them as a table beside the bars, that printed table is the rendering and the bars add nothing to it (see Chart With a Printed Data Grid§9.1.2).

Nothing on the page prints the words start or end, and they MUST NOT be invented as labels of a mark; the pair lives in the row's two period cells.

How a gantt row is laid out. A gantt chart MUST be one table with one row per task bar or milestone, in the chart's top-to-bottom order: the printed label, the start period, the end period. Its header row MUST be Start | End over the two period columns, with the first cell holding the printed label column's title or left empty. These header cells are protocol vocabulary, like the markers [blank] or [logo: …]: the page does not print them, and they are the one deliberate exception to never invent, so that the columns can be read without guessing. They are written exactly as given.

A bar edge on a period boundary. A bar that fills January through March has its right edge on the April tick. Its end MUST be the last period the bar visibly fills (Mar), and one reading MUST be used throughout a document (see Choices Made Once Per Document§4.2). A checker accepts a reading one boundary off.

✅ Sample (constructed) — make_gantt

Four task bars and a diamond milestone on a month axis: five rows, the milestone with start and end both Dec. Design fills January to March and its end is Mar, the last month it fills.

✅ Sample — metro_s2_p18

Four task bars, one milestone and the revenue-service window on a quarter axis under two year headers — six rows in the chart's top-to-bottom order. The Sub Comp 2026 down-triangle is a single-position mark, so start and end are the same quarter; the double-headed RSD 2026 arrow spans the Q4 2026 column, both its edges in one quarter, so it too resolves to one period. A mark whose two edges fall in one quarter still gets its row. The dashed vertical line is a status marker with no label and adds nothing. The labels are printed in bold; the report headings above the chart are elided.

✅ Sample — guideway_schedule_p100

A schedule whose left-hand table prints each activity's ID, name, duration, start and finish: that printed table is the rendering, with its printed dates as the span of each bar, and the bar area to its right — year and quarter headers, bars, bar labels — adds nothing. The table lists 26 activities under group and crew bands. Long names are clipped at the edge of the name column and are written as far as they are visible ((cre on EGCC1270; on EGCC1350 the next letter is cut mid-glyph and left out). The first five activities are shown.

Sankey

A flow's value is the number it carries. Where only node totals are printed, a node with a single inflow or a single outflow gives that one flow its value, and the flow takes the same row shape. A node that both splits and merges has no single flow its total belongs to: its total gives no flow row, and its printed total is kept as text. A sankey that prints no values has no readable flows: ribbon widths MUST NOT be estimated.

Node names in the source and target cells are copied without any printed node total. A ribbon is traced from end to end before its row is written — values often print at the ribbon's start, far from the target node, and a thin ribbon can pass under several others. A ribbon that cannot be traced unambiguously gets no row.

How a sankey flow is laid out. A sankey diagram MUST be one table with one row per flow, ordered by source from top to bottom and then by target, under the header row Source | Target | Value. Each printed node total that is not any one flow's value follows the table as text, as printed (Industry 165). These header cells are protocol vocabulary, like the markers [blank] or [logo: …]: the page does not print them, and they are the one deliberate exception to never invent, so that the columns can be read without guessing. They are written exactly as given.

✅ Sample (constructed) — make_sankey

Every ribbon prints its value: four rows. Coal 120 and Wind 30 each feed a single flow, so their totals are already the flows' values; Gas 130, Industry 165 and Buildings 115 each join or split several flows, and their printed totals follow the table. The (TWh) in the printed title stays in the title. Node labels are printed in bold.

How a checker judges spans and flows

A gantt span and a sankey flow are judged on meaning, not on a table shape: a checker accepts any output that conveys both endpoints of a span at the granularity the axis prints — a positional grid correctly aligned to the periods included — and accepts a span end one period boundary off. A flow is accepted wherever the output conveys its source, its target and its value together. A flow or span whose parts are scattered so that they can no longer be paired is not conveyed.
